Use an extended metaphor involving a common object to illustrate the difference between these approaches.
samples.generated:
The two methods which I have in mind are like the two different kinds of
sawing which were made use of in <PLACE>. In the one case men begin at
the end, and saw from the end backwards to the beginning. In the other
they begin at the beginning, and saw from the beginning forwards to the
end. The end of the saw is the edge which cuts, and the beginning is
the blade which drives the edge against the wood. In the first method,
then, we begin with the edge, and with the sharpness of the cut, and
with the beauty and grace of the cutting; in the other, with the blade
and the dullness and clumsiness of the driving. This explains the reason
why the first method is called “the way of the Spirit,” and the other
“the way of the flesh.” The spirit, when he sees the beauty of the end,
will be very careful that the thing should be done in such a way as
shall make it beautiful; but the man of the flesh, when he has seen
what it is to be done, will try how he can drive it through, without
regard to any consideration of form or fashion or order.

samples.generated:
This kind of superficial appreciation of art is really bad. Take music.
Music is an art, and therefore it is only valuable when you understand the
meaning behind it. It is not valuable as a piece of art, but valuable as an
expression of the feelings of which it is the expression. When you hear
music, you are not listening to the notes, but to the feelings they evoke in
the composer and in the audience. When you hear <PERSON>, it does not
impress you with the music; it impresses you with the tragedy of human
nature. I suppose there would be no music if people had not suffered from
this sort of thing.

The same applies to literature. If you read a poem by <ORG> (I do not
think he wrote many poems) you are not appreciating the poem as a poem,
but as a picture of what was in his heart. He was a man who lived on the
sea, and who was very much like a sea captain himself. That is why he wrote
so many songs about the sea. It is not the poetry that counts, but the
poet. His poetry may be a little weak, but it is a good deal stronger
than the poetry of a man who has never seen the sea.
